item.content:encoded:
Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · post

I live in a nice neighborhood. I will never understand how people that are so well off can be so cheap and mean to household employees. Especially those taking care of your kids and being in your house! Take care of people, folks.


One of my neighbors called me a communist in the street because I said I provide healthcare and pay taxes (you know, don’t pay under the table).


I took it as a compliment.

Nathan Baschez (@nbaschez) · context

that's orange county for you, lol

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

Yeah I’m not in Orange County

karl@ostendorf.com (@chicagokarl) · context

How do you get into that kind of conversation with a neighbor?

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

She was talking mad shit about a nanny (whom she recently fired, one of many), then she complained she was overpaid (she wasn't), and I basically had enough and was like, "well, I pay my person <x> with healthcare" and she was like just flabbergasted.

ተገላቢጦሽ (@flippedgeo) · context

The idea of you being a communist is cracking me up

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

The idea of anyone in this neighborhood (median home price above $5M USD) being a communist... lmao.

Mike Garuccio (@mgaruccio) · context

I’d be pretty offended at being called a communist for recognizing my employees respond to incentives and acting accordingly.


That kinda seems like the entire idea behind capitalism?

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

Yep lol.

Davide (@task_davide) · context

That doesn't really sound like a nice neighborhood

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

This is funny

item.content:encoded:
Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · post

I’ve been asked for an updated daily schedule given Superlogical, second kid, and AI usage. Here you go:


- 530 awake, 20 minute interval cardio

- 600 review nightly agents, start new

- 700 wake and feed newborn

- 730 wake, dress toddler

- 745 breakfast with family

- 800 off to work

- 1200 lunch (often with wife)

- 1530 to 1945 family time

- 2000 hang with wife, start new nightly agents


Early 2026 I mentioned a goal of “always have an agent running” but admitted I was realistically only getting agents for a couple hours off work.


As of today, I’ve gotten a LOT better, I regularly have at least 2 agents running constantly with many running through most of the night. I’ll cover this in more detail another time!

Aleks Kin (@thealekskin) · context

How do you manage to have it running all night or near that? Is it some kinda self-feeding loop with the final goal?

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

Yes to the latter.

faizan khan (@faizan10114) · context

when you run night-agents, what are they running on? which agents?

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

A mix:

- Research

- Trial and error solving a fairly open ended task

- Email triage and planning (no writing or sending)

- Issue triage and bug fixing (no auto-push, but code writing, staged for review)

- Judging the work I did the previous day, adversarial review

Tanvir Raj (@tanvirraj) · context

Hey Mitchell, thanks for writing this!

Ive also 2 child


I’m really curious to know more about how you write your prompts for the nightly agents and what kind of work they do .

In my experience most agent tasks not tend to be pretty long may be one hour to 2/3 hours.

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

A mix:

- Research

- Trial and error solving a fairly open ended task

- Email triage and planning (no writing or sending)

- Issue triage and bug fixing (no auto-push, but code writing, staged for review)

- Judging the work I did the previous day, adversarial review

ezenwa (@turntupjason) · context

how are you people reviewing code of these “many” agents?

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

Pretty much all I do.

Liz Hurder (@valleyfaraday) · context

the only thing unreasonable about this schedule is waking up the newborn at 7am.


(mine was ready to rage at 6am)

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

So far we've produced two good sleepers. Crossing fingers as the newborn continues to grow. Toddler is a rock star.

Axat (@axat_div) · context

Thanks for sharing. As someone that just had a kid, I'm wondering if you outsource any stuff like childcare, cooking, etc. to nannies, chefs, etc. to get some time back? Or do you and your spouse manage all of it?

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

Yes:

- Newborn has a nanny from 8 AM to 330 PM.

- We have a full time housekeeper that does all cleaning, dishes, laundry, car washes, etc. Leaves at 3 PM.

- We have 7 PM to 7 AM night nurses for the new born for now (until they sleep through the night, roughly 4 to 6 months)

- We do most of our own cooking. Parents help some meals (not regularly scheduled, just spontaneously). We have a chef come one night per week for dinner.


The goal with all this is that 330 PM to ~bedtime is private family time. Mornings the kids are usually out anyways.

Matheus Horst (@matheushorst) · context

in general what do you have your agents do?

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

A mix:

- Research

- Trial and error solving a fairly open ended task

- Email triage and planning (no writing or sending)

- Issue triage and bug fixing (no auto-push, but code writing, staged for review)

- Judging the work I did the previous day, adversarial review

Ted Nyman (@tnm) · context

post full cardio routine

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

I just do 30 seconds on, 30 seconds off stationary bike sprints (with a short warmup/cooldown). First thing in the morning. Drink a full bottle of water before breakfast. I lift twice a week otherwise.

Francesco — oss/acc (@ceccon_me) · context

How do you manage social events with such an early schedule? Take the hit on sleep when you go out?

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

I don’t go out. I have no interest, I derive no personal joy from it. Of course on the rare occasion for an obligation like birthday or whatever sure. For the most part we see adult friends with kids on the weekends or afternoons.

Allan MacGregor (@allanmacgregor) · context

you are doing amazing work but there is something deeply sad about your schedule

Matheus Horst (@matheushorst) · context

what do you think is deeply sad about his schedule?

Allan MacGregor (@allanmacgregor) · context

Look at the breakdown, Agents get a full hour, but kids and family 45 minutes max.

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

I think you misread it. Kids aren’t even awake until 7 to 730 and then I spend 330 to 730 pm with the family. Plus the toddler goes to preschool now, so she’s not home after 830 anyways.

item.description: Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · post OSC8 is the terminal sequence for linking arbitrary text (similar to `a` tags in HTML). It is mandatory for a modern terminal experience but prone to malicious use. The next version of Ghostty contains the strongest protections for malici...
item.content:encoded:
Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · post

OSC8 is the terminal sequence for linking arbitrary text (similar to `a` tags in HTML). It is mandatory for a modern terminal experience but prone to malicious use. The next version of Ghostty contains the strongest protections for malicious OSC8 short of disabling it entirely.


In the next version of Ghostty, we've added a classifier for OSC8 URLs (any hidden URL, really) that classifies a URL as: trusted, requires-confirmation, or deny. The screenshots below show the separate requires-confirmation and deny alerts.


We also now show hidden characters in the URL preview in the bottom of the window (previously we interpreted the Unicode directly which allowed maliciously crafted URLs to hide themselves). Hidden characters immediately trigger the `deny` classification, too.


These are the strongest, most comprehensive protections for OSC8 across terminals. As a comparison:


* Alacritty, Kitty, iTerm2, WezTerm: enabled by default with zero filtering at all. Can directly open executables or maliciously crafted schemes without any filter. Can hide the real URL through Unicode tricks.


* Gnome Terminal: enables all OSC8, no configuration I could find to disable. Only rejects remote-host `file://` URLs. No other sanitization, confirmation, etc.


* VS Code Terminal: Allowlist of safe protocols, prompts for unknown, silently replaces whitespace characters. Very good!


* Windows Terminal: Allowlist, prompts for anything executable, prompts for any custom schemes. Very good!

Olivier Mengué (@omengue) · context

I can't even imagine what URL could be marked as trusted except purely ASCII and exactly the same as the displayed text.

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

All http/https is trusted since the preview is visible and browsers have their own security barriers. Local files are trusted if they're non-executable and readable and advertise a text format. etc.

bitwise (@bitwise0x2a) · original

I built Remux, a mobile-first tmux client for iPhone, powered by libghostty.


It uses tmux control mode to bring remote sessions, windows, and panes into a native mobile UI. It's open source and now in beta.


Thanks

@mitchellh

and the Ghostty contributors for making this possible


code:

https://

github.com/h3nock/remux

Rob Pruzan (@robknight__) · context

does it support the kitty graphics protocol?

Mitchell Hashimoto (@mitchellh) · reply

Tmux itself doesn't so it can't unless they forked it. Ghostty supports unicode placeholders (the only terminal other than Kitty too) so compliant Kitty graphics producing applications can use that and it works.
